s06a.slug: WEDNESDAY · 2:20 PM · HOLLIS HALL, THE BACK STEPS
body: The back steps of Hollis are the custodians’ side of the building: a flight of poured concrete going down over the bike racks and a stand of eucalyptus to a piece of the Channel, blue and hammered flat, and at twenty past two the sun is on all of it. The custodians smoke out here in the mornings; in the afternoon the steps belong to whoever finds them. Sixty-something degrees on the second of December. Jack sits three steps from the top with Augustine before the garden still on him and the paperback in his back pocket digging in, and opens the phone, which has been going against his leg since the last ten minutes of seminar.

Dom had a way of letting the end of a sentence go down and die, a sorrowful thing he kept for the Prayers of the Faithful, and it had turned out to be exactly right for a boy who sparkles. Gina on the porch glider with her knees up, refusing for two chapters to laugh at it, and then laughing at it every night till August. Below him a kid walks a bike with a flat up the path, ticking. The phone lies on his knee for three minutes and goes again.

s12a.slug: SATURDAY · 11:40 AM · THE MARINE LAB TURNOUT, OCEAN ROAD

body.text: its daylight. marine lab turnout. 1140. you can ask now

body: There’s a great deal of light at the Marine Lab turnout. He has only ever had the place by a sodium lamp or the moon, or not at all, a chain and a sign at the edge of somebody’s headlights; at twenty to twelve on a Saturday, with his hair still wet from the shower, it turns out to have colors. The chain across the service drive is rust and salt. The sign about the tide pools has a harbor seal painted on it, peeling. The ice plant runs down over the lip of the bluff red at the tips, and past it the Channel is lit all the way out to the islands, so bright he has to take it in pieces, and the gulls on the guardrail stand around in it with their eyes shut.

The Saab is nosed up to the chain with the top down, pinker in the sun than he knew and more dented, a crease down the rear quarter panel he could lay his forearm in and a dimple in the trunk lid the shape of somebody’s knee. A long black garment bag hangs zipped from the passenger headrest, for tonight, and so she isn’t in either seat. She’s sitting up on the back of the car where the top folds down, with her bare feet on the back seat and sunglasses on and her hair wound up in a knot with a yellow pencil stuck through it, and a booklet open on her knees.

He knew about the freckles. He didn’t know there were this many, or that they went on down her neck into the collar of her T-shirt. There’s a tiredness under her eyes from whatever sleep she got, wherever she got it, and the faint crease of a pillowcase still on one cheek. It’s the first time he has seen her in daylight.
She hears his boots on the gravel and takes the sunglasses off to look at him. She looks for a good while.

“I had a theory,” she says. “That it was the dark. Everybody looks better to everybody at two in the morning. It’s a known fact. My entire industry is built on it.” She folds the sunglasses and hooks them in the neck of the T-shirt. “It isn’t the dark.” She says it the way somebody reports good results from a test they were afraid of, and she doesn’t bother hiding that she’s pleased.

She leans down off the back of the car and puts her thumb on his cheekbone, just under the eye, and turns his face to the sun. “You have a freckle. There. I’ve kissed that in the dark about forty times and never seen it.” She lets go of his face. “I’m going to be insufferable about it.”
“You said I could ask.”

“I did say that.” She holds up the booklet. It has the university’s seal on the cover over PRACTICE PROBLEMS, and the corner has gone soft from her thumb, and every page he can see has been erased down to a shine in places. “It’s for the math placement test. They mailed it to me.”
“I’m starting in January,” Skye says. “Here. Spring. Undeclared.” She turns a page. “I’ve declared enough.”
Something gets to his face at *January* and *here*, and he feels it get there, and she sees it. She goes on anyway.
“In Montecito,” he says, “you said not yet.”
“It’s yet.”

He puts a boot up on the bumper, and she moves her feet to make room on the seat, and he sits on the side of the car below her with the booklet between his knee and hers. The page she’s on is fractions. Every problem on it has been tried at least twice.

“I haven’t done math since I was fourteen,” she says. “Not on purpose. On a set you get a studio teacher. It’s the law. Three hours a day, in a trailer, in between setups, twenty minutes at a time.” She pulls the pencil out of her knot, and her hair comes down around her shoulders, and she rubs out an answer with the eraser, hard, while she talks. “Mine was a woman named Irene who knitted socks for her grandchildren in Fresno. She taught me the Louisiana Purchase without dropping a stitch. Every time we got to fractions, somebody knocked on the trailer and said they needed me in five, and Irene would say *go on, honey*, and fractions lost to the light every time. After a while Irene stopped bringing them up.” She blows the eraser crumbs off the page into the back seat. “At sixteen I took a proficiency test, in a trailer in Valencia, on my lunch, so I could be done with school.” She considers the Channel. “I’d never been to one to be done with.”
“You’ve never been in a high school.”

“Not even to vote.” She turns the page back. “And the network’s sending Cassidy away to boarding school in the spring. She’s already *at* a boarding school, there’s a lake, it’s the premise. They’re sending her to a different one. In Switzerland. Off camera.” Her face is bright with it. “So we’re both going off to school. I think that’s the funniest thing that’s ever happened to me, and I’m the only person at the network who does.”
She’s working the eraser again, at a seven-twelfths that isn’t right, and she doesn’t look up from it.

“Sharks were a lie,” she says. “I’ve never been bad at anything where anybody could see my face. I was good at being eleven. I was good at crying on a dock. A few million people watched Cassidy cry on that dock, and I was fine, because I was good at it.” She rubs until the paper pills. “Twenty eighteen-year-olds in a room, watching me get seven-twelfths wrong.” She blows the crumbs off. “I’d take the shark.”
“Show me,” he says.

She hands him the booklet, and after a moment the pencil. He draws a circle in the margin and cuts it into twelve like a pie, the way he did it for Gina at the kitchen table on Glenwood for three winters running, with Nonna saying from the stove that in her day they had used actual pie. He doesn’t hurry it. A fraction is only a thing cut up fair, he tells her; the bottom number is how many pieces, the top is how many you’ve got, and once the knife’s gone in, the bottom number doesn’t change for anybody. He shades seven of the slices, and then three of them over again, and lets her look.

She sees it at once. It was never the math; he can watch it go into her like a key into a lock she’s had the whole time. She takes the pencil back off him and does the next one herself, and the one after, fast, in a hand that slants downhill.
She starts casting them.

“Five-twelfths,” she says to the page, flat, bored, a woman behind a folding table at the end of a long day. “Too tall. *Next.*” Her pencil moves. “Two-thirds. Love what you’re doing. We’re going a different direction.” She circles an answer. “Three-fourths. Thank you so much for coming in, we have your headshot.” She gets every one of them right, and winds her hair back up and runs the pencil through it, and the knot holds.
“You don’t make it a favor,” she says. “When you explain something. Everybody who’s ever explained anything to me did it like they were doing me a favor.”

There are stairs down the bluff below the sign, railroad ties sunk into the ice plant with sand on every tread. She goes down them ahead of him barefoot with the booklet rolled up in her back pocket, and goes out across the rocks at the bottom quick and flat-footed, without looking down, her arms out for balance she doesn’t need. The rocks are black and wet and pocked with pools, each with its own small business going on in it: turban snails, a crab the size of a thumbnail backing away into a crack, a scatter of green anemones folded shut. She crouches over the biggest pool and puts her finger straight into the middle of one, and it closes on her, slowly, all the way to the knuckle.
“It likes me.”
“It’s trying to eat you.”
“Same thing, where I work.”

The rock is cold under her feet and she doesn’t seem to notice it. The sun is all over her, her hair, the freckles, the hand in the pool. He steps across to the next rock to see the anemone better and the rock isn’t where his boot thought it was, and he goes into the pool beside it to the knee, and the Pacific comes in over the top of his boot like a bucket of ice. She laughs so hard the anemone lets go of her.

She kisses him there, with him standing in the pool and her on the rock above it, so that she has to bend down to do it. It’s short. Her mouth is warm and tastes of salt, and there’s salt on his own, and a gull on the next rock over watches all of it with one yellow eye like it paid to get in. She’s laughing at his jeans before it’s over.
He climbs out and sits on a dry rock and pours the Pacific out of his boot. She sits down beside him with her feet in the pool and her face up to the sun and her eyes closed.
“When I said January,” she says, with her eyes still shut, “you did a face.”
He opens his mouth.

“No, I know what it was.” She opens one eye at him. “It’s your church people. Your casserole people. The ones who are going to pray for me. *At* me. Holding hands.” She shuts the eye again. “Your church people are going to hate me.”
“It isn’t —”
“It’s fine. I’m very easy to hate in person. It’s a gift.” The sun is on her eyelids. She lifts her finger out of the water to look at it, and puts it back in to see if anything else will have her.

response: She opens her eyes and turns her head to look at him in the sun without the glasses, the freckles and the tired and the salt drying white on her ankles. “In daylight,” she says. “You said that in daylight.”

response: At ten to one a marimba goes off in her back pocket, and she says a word Cassidy isn’t allowed to say. Two hours and change to LA, hair at four, and a white piano going around in a swimming pool waiting for her to stand next to it in something. She goes up the bluff stairs ahead of him, the booklet back in her fist, and leaves wet footprints on the sand on every tie, and at the top she drops into the driver’s seat beside the garment bag and starts the Saab and backs it around in the gravel, spraying a little of it at the gulls. She points the booklet at him out of the open car, which could mean anything, and goes south with the top down and her hair coming loose in the wind. The turnout is empty at five to one with all of its light still in it, and he’s standing there in jeans gone stiff with salt to the knee, and the gulls come back down onto the guardrail one at a time.
